messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was nineteen when the tornado came through his hometown near Springfield, Illinois, on a March evening in 2023. He had been working his shift at the McDonald's on Route 66 when the manager told everyone to get away from the windows. Marcus remembered the sound first—not the wind itself but the roar beneath it, something alive and hungry. He remembered the smell of ozone and wet soil pouring through the ventilation system. The building shook. A customer screamed. Then, in the chaos of the evacuation, Marcus found himself separated from the group, pressed into a storage closet with two other employees, listening to what sounded like the world tearing apart outside. When the noise stopped and they emerged, the parking lot was unrecognizable—cars overturned, debris everywhere, a utility pole snapped like kindling. Marcus had walked away physically unharmed, but something in him had fractured in that closet.

In the months that followed, Marcus noticed changes he couldn't quite name. The vividness of his memories disturbed him most. When he tried to recall the event—and he found himself trying constantly, as though understanding it better might make it less real—the images came back sharp and complete. He could see the fluorescent lights flickering, the crack spreading across the ceiling tile, the faces of his coworkers frozen in fear. Worse was the sensory intrusion: when these images surfaced, often unbidden, he could smell the ozone again, could taste the dust that had settled on his tongue. The terror came back too, not as a thought but as a physical sensation, his chest tightening, his breath shortening, his body convinced it was happening again.

Marcus had started rehearsing conversations weeks before his first therapy appointment. Before his shift, he would stand in his bedroom and whisper through interactions with customers, managers, other employees—scripting every word, every inflection, terrified that if he wasn't prepared, something would go wrong. At work, he'd arrive early to mentally map the building, identifying exits, calculating distances, checking weather forecasts obsessively. His manager had noticed him becoming withdrawn and unreliable. Twice he'd called in sick when the forecast mentioned thunderstorms. Once, when a customer raised their voice about a wrong order, Marcus had felt his body flood with panic and had to step into the back room to breathe.

Beyond the rehearsal and avoidance, Marcus had begun trying to suppress the memories themselves. When an image surfaced—the crack in the ceiling, the smell of ozone—he would shake his head hard, as though he could physically dislodge it, or he would turn up music, scroll through his phone, do anything to interrupt the thought. But the memories kept returning, more insistent each time he tried to push them away.

What troubled Marcus most, though, was not the memories or the panic but the person he had become in their wake. He used to be someone who joked around at work, who made plans with friends on weekends, who felt generally okay about his life. Now he was someone who couldn't leave his house without a script, who cancelled plans because the idea of being anywhere unpredictable made his stomach turn, who felt a constant, grinding misery that had become so familiar it seemed permanent. He had come to believe that the tornado hadn't just passed through his town—it had passed through him, and what remained was damaged in a way that couldn't be repaired. His friends had tried to reach out, but he'd withdrawn from them. His parents worried. He worried most of all.

Marcus finally made an appointment after his manager pulled him aside and said his performance was suffering, that he needed to "get help or find another job." Sitting in the waiting room, Marcus felt the familiar knot of dread. He was certain that talking about it would only make the memories sharper, the terror more real. But he was also certain that he couldn't keep living like this—rehearsing, avoiding, suppressing, drowning in the person he'd become. He needed to know if the person he used to be was still somewhere inside, or if the tornado had taken that too.
